import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 1133

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/1133](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1133)
- [Er67] Erdős, P., Problems and results on the convergence and divergence properties of the
  Lagrange interpolation polynomials and some extremal problems. Mathematica (Cluj) (1967), 65-73.
-/

open Filter Set

namespace Erdos1133

/--
Let $C>0$. There exists $\epsilon>0$ such that if $n$ is sufficiently large the following holds.

For any $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in [-1,1]$ there exist $y_1,\ldots,y_n\in [-1,1]$ such that, if $P$ is a
polynomial of degree $m<(1+\epsilon)n$ with $P(x_i)=y_i$ for at least $(1-\epsilon)n$ many
$1\leq i\leq n$, then $$\max_{x\in [-1,1]}\lvert P(x)\rvert >C.$$
-/
@[category research open, AMS 26 41]
theorem erdos_1133 :
    answer(sorry) ↔
    ∀ C > (0 : ℝ), ∃ ε > (0 : ℝ), ∀ᶠ n : ℕ in atTop,
      ∀ x : Fin n → Icc (-1 : ℝ) 1,
        ∃ y : Fin n → Icc (-1 : ℝ) 1,
          ∀ P : Polynomial ℝ,
            (P.natDegree : ℝ) < (1 + ε) * (n : ℝ) →
            ((Finset.univ.filter (fun i ↦ P.eval (x i : ℝ) = (y i : ℝ))).card : ℝ) ≥
              (1 - ε) * (n : ℝ) →
            ∃ z ∈ Icc (-1 : ℝ) 1, |P.eval z| > C := by
  sorry

/--
Erdős proved that, for any $C>0$, there exists $\epsilon>0$ such that if $n$ is sufficiently
large and $m=\lfloor (1+\epsilon)n\rfloor$ then for any $x_1,\ldots,x_m\in [-1,1]$ there is a
polynomial $P$ of degree $n$ such that $\lvert P(x_i)\rvert\leq 1$ for $1\leq i\leq m$ and
$\max_{x\in [-1,1]}\lvert P(x)\rvert>C$. The conjectured statement would also imply this, but
Erdős in [Er67] says he could not even prove it for $m=n$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 26 41]
theorem erdos_1133.variants.weaker :
    ∀ C > (0 : ℝ), ∃ ε > (0 : ℝ), ∀ᶠ n : ℕ in atTop,
      let m := ⌊(1 + ε) * (n : ℝ)⌋₊;
      ∀ x : Fin m → Icc (-1 : ℝ) 1,
        ∃ P : Polynomial ℝ,
          P.natDegree = n ∧
          (∀ i : Fin m, |P.eval (x i : ℝ)| ≤ 1) ∧
          ∃ z ∈ Icc (-1 : ℝ) 1, |P.eval z| > C := by
  sorry

end Erdos1133

reformulations.difference: The original paper specifies ordered, distinct interpolation nodes. Lean permits arbitrary tuples, including repeated nodes, as does the modern problem page.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The arbitrary-tuple version immediately implies the distinct-node version. Conversely, take a distinct-node witness δ with 0 < δ ≤ 1 and set ε = δ/4. For an n-tuple with r distinct nodes, if r < (1−ε)n, choose pairwise distinct ordinates: every polynomial then matches at most r indices, so the implication holds vacuously. Otherwise apply the distinct-node conjecture to the r distinct nodes and assign its ordinate to every copy of each node. Matching at least (1−ε)n indices entails matching at least r−εn ≥ (1−δ)r distinct nodes. Moreover, (1+ε)n ≤ (1+δ)r, so the degree bound transfers. Since r ≥ n/2, sufficiently large n guarantees that the distinct-node result applies. Thus the full asymptotic statements are equivalent. The parameter inequalities and monotonicity under shrinking ε were checked in Lean; the full equivalence was not formalized.

reformulations.difference: Theorem 4 in the original paper uses ordered, distinct sample points; Lean and the modern problem page allow repeated and unordered points.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For any m-tuple, extend its set of distinct values to a set of exactly m distinct points in [-1,1], which is possible because the interval is infinite, and order those points. A polynomial bounded by 1 at all points of this enlarged set satisfies every original sampling constraint, with its degree and large-value conclusion unchanged. The converse follows by restricting to distinct tuples. The empty tuple causes no exception.

review.notes: Both declarations match the archived problem page and the corresponding statements on p. 72 of the primary paper. The current companion dataset still records problem 1133 as open, and the source identifies the weaker variant as proved. Live access to the problem page and forum was blocked, so current forum comments could not be checked. Experiments in /workspace/review/scratch.lean compiled without errors: they checked n=0 and n=1, zero-polynomial degree conventions, floor values and nonnegativity, finite-index counting, and exclusion of ε≥1 as a vacuous witness. A Lean proof confirms that the existential large-value conclusion is equivalent to an attained maximum exceeding C on the compact interval. The reviewed file matches the specified commit; no repository files were modified by this review.
